Which rain gauge the river answers to

Source: R/gauge_response.R
gauge_response.Rd

Takes each rain gauge on its own and asks how closely the river's quick response follows it, over the whole record and flood by flood. It is a check made before calibrating, from the records alone: no model is run.

Usage

gauge_response(
  gauges,
  flow,
  time = NULL,
  dt = 1,
  rain = NULL,
  area_km2 = NULL,
  max_lag_h = 48,
  lead_h = 6,
  floods = 20,
  dry_mm = 5,
  events = NULL
)

Arguments

gauges

A data frame or matrix of rain, mm per step, one column per gauge, named. Missing readings are allowed.

flow

Observed flow, m3/s, the same length as the rows of gauges.

time

Optional time stamps, for the event table.

dt

Step length, hours.

rain

Catchment rain for finding the events, mm per step. The mean of the gauges by default.

area_km2

Catchment area, km2, for the event quick flow. Without it size_r uses the peak flow.

max_lag_h

Longest lag tried, hours.

lead_h

Longest negative lag tried, hours: rain recorded after the rise it caused.

floods

How many of the largest events, by peak flow, to judge flood by flood; NULL for every event.

dry_mm

Event rain at the other gauges above which a near-empty gauge counts as dry.

events

Events from find_events(), if already found on the same record.

Value

A pdm_gauge_response list: summary, one row per gauge as described above; events, one row per event with its winner and each gauge's rain (mm) and correlation; correlation, the cross-correlations by gauge, part and lag, for plot().

Details

The fast response. The rise in flow from one step to the next is moved almost only by quick runoff, so the correlation of a gauge's rain with the rise a few steps later measures how well that gauge explains the spikes. lag_h is the lag of the strongest correlation, r its value.

Why not the slow response. Baseflow answers to the rain of many storms over days or weeks, and over such spans the gauges' totals converge: a correlation of gauge rain with baseflow comes out much the same for every gauge, whichever drives it. Long-term drift between gauges is a matter for the double-mass curve of water_balance().

Flood by flood. For each of the floods largest events found on the catchment rain, by peak flow, each gauge's rain is correlated with the rise in flow across the event, at that gauge's own fast lag; the gauge with the highest correlation wins the event. event_wins counts the wins, event_share gives them as a share of the events with a winner. size_r is the correlation, across events, of a gauge's event rain with the event's quick flow: whether the gauge sees the big storms as big. dry_events counts events where a gauge recorded under a tenth of the median gauge, when that median is at least dry_mm: a funnel blocked, a logger down, or a storm that missed the gauge. A storm over one gauge alone leaves the median low and flags nobody.

Reading it. A gauge with a clearly higher r and most of the wins drives the spike. Rain cannot follow the flow it causes, so a negative best lag means the gauge's clock is late, or the flow's early; a gauge whose lag differs from its neighbours' by a whole number of hours points the same way. A gauge with no wins, a low size_r or many dry events is worth checking against its neighbours and the map. Correlations between rain gauges blur the differences, as they do in any cross-correlation analysis (Larocque et al., 1998): read the ranking and the gaps between gauges, not the values alone.

References

Larocque, M., Mangin, A., Razack, M. and Banton, O. (1998). Contribution of correlation and spectral analyses to the regional study of a large karst aquifer (Charente, France). Journal of Hydrology, 205, 217-231. doi:10.1016/S0022-1694(97)00155-8

See also

find_events(), water_balance()

Examples

river <- synthetic_catchment(years = 1, dt = 1, seed = 1)
set.seed(1)
gauges <- data.frame(a = river$forcing$rain * stats::rlnorm(nrow(river$forcing), 0, 0.3),
                     b = river$forcing$rain * stats::rlnorm(nrow(river$forcing), 0, 0.6))
gauge_response(gauges, river$observed, river$forcing$time, area_km2 = river$truth$area_km2)
#> Gauge response: 2 gauges, 20 events
#>  gauge lag_h    r event_wins event_share size_r dry_events
#>      a     2 0.56         17        0.85   0.60          0
#>      b     2 0.48          3        0.15   0.44          0
